input: In this tutorial, we will explore two closely related ideas that are fundamental to making good measurements: absolute error and relative error. We will work through them using a pressure measurement as our example. Suppose that an instrument gives a reading of 230 units, and suppose that the instrument has a tolerance of 0.5% of reading. The absolute error is the size of the error expressed in the units of the measurement itself, and in this case it is worked out as 230 x 0.5 / 100, which gives an absolute error of 1.15 units. The relative error, by contrast, expresses the same error as a fraction or percentage of the reading, which makes it much easier to compare errors across instruments of different sizes. It is also very important to distinguish error from uncertainty. Although the two terms are often used interchangeably in everyday language, they do not mean the same thing: the error is the difference between a measured value and the true value, whereas the uncertainty is an expression of the doubt that remains about the result. Keeping these ideas separate will help you to interpret measurements correctly and to avoid overstating what an instrument can actually tell you. An absolute error of 1.15 units is a statement about the reading in hand, and it should be reported alongside the reading rather than left for the reader to reconstruct from a percentage. With practice, stating both forms becomes routine, and the distinction between them, and between error and uncertainty, stops needing to be thought about at all.
target: This tutorial explains absolute and relative error through a pressure measurement, and keeps error separate from uncertainty. Work through the example and you will be able to state the error on a reading in units and as a percentage of the reading. Take a reading of 230 units from an instrument with a tolerance of 0.5% of reading. The absolute error is the error stated in the units of the measurement. It is calculated as 230 x 0.5 / 100, which gives 1.15 units. The reading therefore stands within 1.15 units of the value it reports, at the stated tolerance. The relative error is the same error divided by the reading, stated as a fraction or a percentage; it carries no units, and it is the form that compares across instruments of different sizes. Error and uncertainty are different terms and are not merged here. Error is a difference: the measured value minus the true value, or the bound the tolerance places on that difference. Uncertainty is the doubt that remains about the result after the measurement is made. A reading with a small stated error can still carry a large uncertainty when the conditions of the measurement are poorly known, and the two statements answer different questions. Uncertainty gathers every source of doubt about the result, the tolerance of the instrument among them, and it is expressed as an interval around the result rather than as a single difference. The tolerance in this example is stated as a percentage of the reading, and the basis matters: a percentage of the reading grows with the reading, where a percentage of full scale would not. Which form of the error to report depends on the use made of the reading. State the absolute error where the reading is checked against a limit expressed in units, and the relative error where readings from instruments of different sizes are compared. Report the error with the reading itself; a reading reported without its error claims more than the instrument establishes.
